title: Give me truth
hookLine: Thoreau: rather than love, money, fame, give me truth
carry: truth before love, money and fame
tomorrow: the sun is a morning star
last: PERHAPS THE SLOW ONE HEARS A DIFFERENT DRUMMER.

cards: Set them on a table in front of a stranger, ask them to pick one, and you'd learn a lot about the stranger. A love song picks the first. A business plan, the second.

A talent show, the third. A few pages from the end of Walden, Thoreau pushes all three aside and asks for something that doesn't fit on the table at all. It's one short sentence, and it puts love on the losing side.

teach.b: The sentence, from Walden's Conclusion: "Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth." First, the shock of the list. Money and fame are easy to set aside in a book about a cabin.
But love? He doesn't say love is bad. He says that if he had to choose, he'd take truth first, maybe because love built on a pretense isn't quite love.

teach.h: A RICH TABLE, AND HE LEFT HUNGRY.
teach.b: Right after the line, he tells of a table with rich food, plenty of wine and attentive service, where sincerity and truth were missing. He went away hungry. A full plate, and he left hungry.
That's how he measures a meal: not by what was served, but by whether anyone was honest at it. Third, what truth means to him here.

teach.h: SAY WHAT YOU HAVE TO SAY.
teach.b: A little earlier in the chapter he writes, "Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe." For Thoreau, truth isn't mainly a fact you look up.
It's the difference between a real life and a performed one. Fourth, the cost. Choosing truth over love, money and fame means some rooms get colder, and some tables you leave early.
He'd rather go home hungry than stay full on make-believe. Readers are free to argue with him, but the line is plain about where he stood.

how: Readers of Walden often hold this line up as Thoreau's case for sincerity: saying what is actually so, even when the expected answer would be more comfortable.

o: Thoreau's choice of truth ahead of love, money and fame
a promise to swear honestly before a court of law
a prayer asking God to reveal the hidden future

games.q: inside the sentence: tap the pairs.

s: he only says that, given the choice, he'd take truth first.
Thoreau left a rich dinner hungry because sincerity was missing
the food and wine were plenty; truth was not.
Thoreau wrote that any truth is better than make-believe
"say what you have to say, not what you ought."

games.q: you're at a table with rich food, fine wine and attentive service, but nobody is being sincere. what does Thoreau do?
games.why: he says he went away hungry: a full plate, but no sincerity or truth at the table.

practice: Let one place come to mind where you say what you ought instead of what you have to say: a meeting, a family dinner, a friendship where something has gone unsaid.
Don't rehearse a speech; just find the one true sentence underneath, short and kind, and say it silently a few times. Notice how it sits.

wordCard.voice: Give me truth. Thoreau's choice, ahead of love, money and fame, and his reason for leaving a rich table hungry. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: truth before love, money and fame. A full plate is no meal if nobody at the table is honest. Rest well.
